planting.note: Set out container plants in spring or early fall so roots establish before summer heat or winter cold; space along low borders or as a dense groundcover mass since individual plants stay quite small.

directions: This is the true dwarf selection distinct from the similarly-named 'Nana Purpurea' — 'Nana' stays lower and denser, with finely divided leaflets that emerge coppery-green and shift to pinkish-red tones through winter. It rarely produces the berries that make straight-species Nandina domestica a concern in mild-winter regions, making it a lower-risk choice near woodland edges or waterways where the species has naturalized. Grow in well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates for the best foliage color, and shear lightly in late winter only to remove tattered growth since flowering and color occur on old wood. Established plants tolerate short dry spells but hold color and density best with occasional deep watering during summer heat.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sprinter (sold under this trade name) fills in noticeably faster than most boxwood selections, making it useful where a finished hedge or mass planting is wanted sooner.

directions: Sprinter is a sport of the popular Winter Gem boxwood, selected for a noticeably quicker growth rate, denser branching, and a slightly more upright habit than its parent, while keeping the same small, glossy, dark-green foliage that resists bronzing better than English boxwood through winter cold. It carries good resistance to boxwood blight and tolerates boxwood leafminer pressure better than many older cultivars, which has made it a popular replacement where blight has damaged existing plantings. Give it well-drained soil, since like all boxwood it is prone to root rot in soggy or heavy clay sites, and site it with afternoon shade in the hottest parts of its range to keep the foliage from bleaching. Light shearing after the spring flush keeps the naturally dense habit tight and formal, though it also holds a good shape with minimal pruning.
